# Introduction

Home Credit provides consumer financing to applicants who may have limited or no traditional credit history. The goal of this project is to develop a predictive model that identifies applicants who are more likely to experience payment difficulties.

The exploratory data analysis (EDA) showed that approximately 8.1% of applicants experienced payment difficulties. This creates a class imbalance problem because most applicants belong to the non-default group.

This modeling analysis will establish a benchmark, compare several classification models, evaluate performance using cross-validation and ROC AUC, investigate class imbalance, and select a final model for predicting payment difficulties.

ROC AUC will be the primary evaluation metric because accuracy alone can be misleading when the target classes are imbalanced.

## Executive Overview

This analysis evaluates how applicant, affordability, and historical credit/repayment information can support lending decisions by ranking the risk of recorded payment difficulties. It compares several classification approaches, then develops a final 36-predictor binomial logistic-regression model that combines application features, aggregated historical information, and three external-score variables.

The final model achieved a mean five-fold ROC AUC of **0.7481** on 307,511 training applications. This level of discrimination can help lending teams distinguish relatively higher- from lower-risk applications for review, but it does not by itself establish an approval policy, calibrated probabilities, or production readiness.

# Data Preparation

The modeling workflow uses the existing `data_preparation.R` script developed from the EDA findings.

The preparation steps include cleaning unusual values, creating applicant age and employment-duration features, calculating financial ratios, and preserving missingness information. The script also uses training-derived parameters to apply consistent transformations to the training and test datasets.

Additional preprocessing required by individual models will be fitted using training data only to avoid data leakage.
```{r}
# Load required packages
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
library(pROC)
library(rpart)
library(ranger)

# Load our existing preparation functions
source("data_preparation.R")

# Read application datasets
train_data <- read_csv(
  "Data/application_train.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

test_data <- read_csv(
  "Data/application_test.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Learn preparation parameters from training data
prep_parameters <- learn_preparation_parameters(train_data)

# Prepare both datasets
train_prepared <- prepare_application_data(
  train_data,
  prep_parameters
)

test_prepared <- prepare_application_data(
  test_data,
  prep_parameters
)

# Check dataset dimensions
dim(train_prepared)
dim(test_prepared)
```

# Modeling Process

## Benchmark: Majority-Class Classifier

The first step is to establish a benchmark using a majority-class classifier. Because approximately 91.9% of applicants did not experience payment difficulties, this classifier predicts that every applicant belongs to the non-default group.

This benchmark helps determine whether more advanced models provide meaningful improvements over simply predicting the most common outcome.

```{r}
# Calculate the majority class
majority_class <- as.integer(
  names(which.max(table(train_prepared$TARGET)))
)

# Predict the majority class for every applicant
benchmark_predictions <- rep(
  majority_class,
  nrow(train_prepared)
)

# Calculate benchmark accuracy
benchmark_accuracy <- mean(
  benchmark_predictions == train_prepared$TARGET
)

# A constant-score classifier has ROC AUC of 0.50
benchmark_auc <- 0.50

# Display benchmark performance
tibble(
  Model = "Majority Class Benchmark",
  Accuracy = benchmark_accuracy,
  AUC = benchmark_auc
)
```

## Logistic Regression

Logistic regression estimates the probability that an applicant will experience payment difficulties. This first model uses applicant age, income, credit amount, annuity amount, and two engineered financial ratios.

Stratified five-fold cross-validation is used to estimate out-of-sample ROC AUC while maintaining approximately the same proportion of payment difficulties in each fold.

```{r}
set.seed(6812)

# Select a manageable sample for initial model comparison
model_data <- train_prepared |>
  select(
    TARGET,
    AGE_YEARS,
    AMT_INCOME_TOTAL,
    AMT_CREDIT,
    AMT_ANNUITY,
    ANNUITY_INCOME_RATIO,
    CREDIT_GOODS_RATIO
  ) |>
  mutate(TARGET = as.integer(TARGET)) |>
  filter(
    if_all(
      -TARGET,
      ~ !is.na(.) & is.finite(.)
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(TARGET) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 10000 / nrow(train_prepared)) |>
  ungroup()

# Create stratified cross-validation folds
folds <- vfold_cv(
  model_data,
  v = 5,
  strata = TARGET
)

# Train and evaluate within each fold
logistic_auc <- map_dbl(folds$splits, function(split) {

  training <- analysis(split)
  validation <- assessment(split)

  model <- glm(
    TARGET ~ .,
    data = training,
    family = binomial()
  )

  probabilities <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = validation,
    type = "response"
  )

  as.numeric(
    auc(
      roc(
        validation$TARGET,
        probabilities,
        quiet = TRUE,
        direction = "<"
      )
    )
  )
})

# Report cross-validation performance
tibble(
  Model = "Logistic Regression",
  Mean_AUC = mean(logistic_auc),
  SD_AUC = sd(logistic_auc)
)
```
The logistic regression model achieved a mean five-fold cross-validation AUC of 0.602, with a standard deviation of 0.0329. This exceeds the majority-class benchmark AUC of 0.50, indicating that the model provides some ability to distinguish applicants who experience payment difficulties. However, its performance remains modest, suggesting that more flexible models and additional predictors should be explored.

## Decision Tree

```{r}
# Use the same cross-validation folds as logistic regression
# so the model comparison is consistent.

decision_tree_auc <- purrr::map_dbl(folds$splits, function(split) {

  training <- rsample::analysis(split)
  validation <- rsample::assessment(split)

  # Train a decision tree classifier
  model <- rpart::rpart(
    factor(TARGET) ~ .,
    data = training,
    method = "class",
    control = rpart::rpart.control(
      cp = 0.001,
      minsplit = 20,
      maxdepth = 5
    )
  )

  # Predict probability of payment difficulty (TARGET = 1)
  probabilities <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = validation,
    type = "prob"
  )[, "1"]

  # Calculate validation AUC
  as.numeric(
    pROC::auc(
      pROC::roc(
        response = validation$TARGET,
        predictor = probabilities,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        direction = "<",
        quiet = TRUE
      )
    )
  )
})

# Display cross-validation results
tibble(
  Model = "Decision Tree",
  Mean_AUC = mean(decision_tree_auc),
  SD_AUC = sd(decision_tree_auc)
)
```
The decision tree achieved a mean five-fold cross-validation AUC of 0.505, with a standard deviation of 0.0117. This is only slightly above the benchmark AUC of 0.50 and substantially below the logistic regression AUC of 0.602. Under the current predictor selection and model settings, the decision tree does not provide a meaningful improvement. Logistic regression remains the stronger candidate for further evaluation.

## Random Forest
```{r}
# Use the same five cross-validation folds as previous models
# for a fair comparison.

set.seed(6812)

random_forest_auc <- purrr::map_dbl(folds$splits, function(split) {

  training <- rsample::analysis(split) |>
  mutate(TARGET = factor(TARGET, levels = c(0, 1)))

validation <- rsample::assessment(split) |>
  mutate(TARGET = factor(TARGET, levels = c(0, 1)))

  # Train a random forest with 100 trees
  model <- ranger::ranger(
    TARGET ~ .,
    data = training,
    num.trees = 100,
    mtry = 3,
    min.node.size = 10,
    probability = TRUE,
    seed = 6812
  )

  # Predict probability of payment difficulty (TARGET = 1)
  probabilities <- predict(
    model,
    data = validation
  )$predictions[, "1"]

  # Calculate validation AUC
  as.numeric(
    pROC::auc(
      pROC::roc(
        response = validation$TARGET,
        predictor = probabilities,
        levels = c(0, 1),
        direction = "<",
        quiet = TRUE
      )
    )
  )
})

# Display cross-validation results
tibble(
  Model = "Random Forest",
  Mean_AUC = mean(random_forest_auc),
  SD_AUC = sd(random_forest_auc)
)
```

## Model Performance Comparison

The three candidate models were evaluated using five-fold stratified cross-validation on the same sample.

Logistic Regression achieved the highest mean AUC (0.602), followed by Random Forest (0.567) and Decision Tree (0.505). All three models were compared against the majority-class benchmark AUC of 0.500.

Logistic Regression is currently the strongest candidate. However, its performance is still modest, so additional experiments with class imbalance and hyperparameter tuning are needed before selecting a final model.

## Addressing Class Imbalance

The Home Credit training dataset is highly imbalanced, with approximately 8.1% of applicants experiencing payment difficulties.

To investigate whether balancing the classes improves predictive performance, I will compare the original Logistic Regression model with a model trained using class weights.

Class weights give greater importance to the minority class (TARGET = 1) during model training. Both models will be evaluated using the same five-fold cross-validation splits and ROC AUC metric.

```{r}
# Compare weighted and unweighted logistic regression
# Use the same five cross-validation folds for a fair comparison

weighted_logistic_auc <- purrr::map_dbl(
  folds$splits,
  function(split) {

    # Separate training and validation data
    training <- rsample::analysis(split)
    validation <- rsample::assessment(split)

    # Calculate class frequencies using training data only
    n_0 <- sum(training$TARGET == 0)
    n_1 <- sum(training$TARGET == 1)

    # Give higher weights to the minority class
    training$case_weight <- ifelse(
      training$TARGET == 1,
      nrow(training) / (2 * n_1),
      nrow(training) / (2 * n_0)
    )

    # Store weights separately
fold_weights <- training$case_weight

# Remove weights from predictor data
training_model <- training |>
  dplyr::select(-case_weight)

# Fit weighted logistic regression
model <- glm(
  TARGET ~ .,
  data = training_model,
  family = binomial(),
  weights = fold_weights
)

    # Predict probabilities on validation data
    probabilities <- predict(
      model,
      newdata = validation,
      type = "response"
    )

    # Calculate validation ROC AUC
    as.numeric(
      pROC::auc(
        pROC::roc(
          response = validation$TARGET,
          predictor = probabilities,
          levels = c(0, 1),
          direction = "<",
          quiet = TRUE
        )
      )
    )
  }
)

# Compare original and weighted logistic regression
tibble(
  Model = c(
    "Original Logistic Regression",
    "Weighted Logistic Regression"
  ),
  Mean_AUC = c(
    mean(logistic_auc),
    mean(weighted_logistic_auc)
  )
)
```
Class weighting was tested to address the imbalance between applicants with and without payment difficulties. Both the original and weighted Logistic Regression models achieved a mean cross-validation ROC AUC of approximately 0.602. This suggests that class weighting did not meaningfully improve the model's ability to distinguish between the two groups. Therefore, the original Logistic Regression remains the preferred candidate at this stage.

## Hyperparameter Tuning

Random Forest hyperparameters were tuned to investigate whether adjusting model complexity improves predictive performance. A stratified sample of the prepared training data was used to reduce computation time. Three-fold cross-validation was used to compare candidate settings based on ROC AUC.
```{r}
# Tune Random Forest using a manageable sample
set.seed(6812)

tuning_data <- model_data |>
  dplyr::group_by(TARGET) |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(prop = 5000 / nrow(model_data)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

# Create three stratified cross-validation folds
tuning_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(
  tuning_data,
  v = 3,
  strata = TARGET
)

# Randomly select six hyperparameter combinations
tuning_grid <- tidyr::crossing(
  mtry = c(2, 3, 4, 5),
  min.node.size = c(5, 10, 20)
) |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 6)

# Evaluate each combination
tuning_results <- purrr::pmap_dfr(
  tuning_grid,
  function(mtry, min.node.size) {

    fold_auc <- purrr::map_dbl(
      tuning_folds$splits,
      function(split) {

        training <- rsample::analysis(split)
        validation <- rsample::assessment(split)

        model <- ranger::ranger(
          TARGET ~ .,
          data = training,
          num.trees = 100,
          mtry = mtry,
          min.node.size = min.node.size,
          probability = TRUE,
          seed = 6812
        )

        probabilities <- predict(
  model,
  data = validation
)$predictions[, 2]

        as.numeric(
          pROC::auc(
            pROC::roc(
              response = validation$TARGET,
              predictor = probabilities,
              levels = c(0, 1),
              direction = "<",
              quiet = TRUE
            )
          )
        )
      }
    )

    tibble(
      mtry = mtry,
      min.node.size = min.node.size,
      Mean_AUC = mean(fold_auc),
      SD_AUC = sd(fold_auc)
    )
  }
)

# Show configurations ranked by AUC
tuning_results |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Mean_AUC))
```
Six Random Forest hyperparameter configurations were evaluated using three-fold cross-validation. The highest mean ROC AUC was 0.557, achieved with mtry = 2 and min.node.size = 20. Although tuning identified the best configuration among those tested, the tuned Random Forest did not outperform the original Logistic Regression model, which achieved an AUC of 0.602. Therefore, Logistic Regression remains the preferred model based on the current results.

## Final Model Training

Logistic Regression was selected as the final model candidate because it achieved the highest cross-validation ROC AUC among the models evaluated. Class weighting did not meaningfully improve its performance, and Random Forest hyperparameter tuning did not produce a stronger result.

The final Logistic Regression model will be trained using the full prepared training dataset and used to generate predicted probabilities for the Kaggle test dataset.

```{r}
# Select the same predictors used during model comparison
final_predictors <- c(
  "AGE_YEARS",
  "AMT_INCOME_TOTAL",
  "AMT_CREDIT",
  "AMT_ANNUITY",
  "ANNUITY_INCOME_RATIO",
  "CREDIT_GOODS_RATIO"
)

# Prepare full training data
final_train <- train_prepared |>
  dplyr::select(TARGET, dplyr::all_of(final_predictors)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(TARGET = as.integer(TARGET)) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    dplyr::if_all(
      -TARGET,
      ~ !is.na(.) & is.finite(.)
    )
  )

# Train final logistic regression model
final_model <- glm(
  TARGET ~ .,
  data = final_train,
  family = binomial()
)

# Report number of observations used
tibble::tibble(
  Model = "Final Logistic Regression",
  Training_Observations = nrow(final_train)
)
```

## Kaggle Submission

The final Logistic Regression model is used to predict the probability of payment difficulty for applicants in the test dataset. Missing predictor values are handled using median values calculated from the training data.
```{r}
# Prepare test predictors
final_test <- test_prepared |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(final_predictors))

# Calculate medians using training data only
train_medians <- vapply(
  final_train[final_predictors],
  median,
  numeric(1),
  na.rm = TRUE
)

# Replace missing or non-finite test values
for (column in final_predictors) {
  invalid <- !is.finite(final_test[[column]])
  final_test[[column]][invalid] <- train_medians[[column]]
}

# Generate predicted probabilities
test_probabilities <- predict(
  final_model,
  newdata = final_test,
  type = "response"
)

# Create Kaggle submission
submission <- tibble::tibble(
  SK_ID_CURR = test_prepared$SK_ID_CURR,
  TARGET = as.numeric(test_probabilities)
)

# Verify submission
stopifnot(
  nrow(submission) == nrow(test_prepared),
  !anyNA(submission$TARGET),
  all(submission$TARGET >= 0 & submission$TARGET <= 1)
)

# Save submission locally
readr::write_csv(submission, "kaggle_submission.csv")

# Display first six predictions
head(submission)
```

## Supplementary Data Experiment: Bureau Credit History

The baseline Logistic Regression model used six predictors from
the application dataset and achieved a cross-validation ROC AUC
of 0.602.

This experiment investigates whether adding historical credit
information from bureau.csv improves predictive performance.

### Prepare Bureau-Enhanced Data

```{r}
# Load Bureau data and create applicant-level features
bureau <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/bureau.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

bureau_features <- aggregate_bureau_data(bureau)

# Join Bureau features to application data
train_bureau <- train_prepared |>
  dplyr::left_join(bureau_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR")

# Check that no applicants were duplicated
stopifnot(nrow(train_bureau) == nrow(train_prepared))

# Inspect the enhanced dataset
dim(train_bureau)
```

### Logistic Regression with Bureau Features

This experiment adds four credit-history features to the six
predictors used in the baseline Logistic Regression model.

The enhanced model will be evaluated using five-fold
cross-validation to compare its performance with the baseline.

```{r}
# Combine original predictors with Bureau features
bureau_predictors <- c(
  final_predictors,
  "BUREAU_LOAN_COUNT",
  "BUREAU_ACTIVE_COUNT",
  "BUREAU_TOTAL_DEBT",
  "BUREAU_MAX_OVERDUE_DAYS"
)

# Prepare data for the enhanced model
bureau_model_data <- train_bureau |>
  dplyr::select(TARGET, dplyr::all_of(bureau_predictors)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(TARGET = as.integer(TARGET))

# Check missing values in the new features
colSums(is.na(bureau_model_data))
```

### Create a Matched Bureau Comparison Sample

The original modeling sample is reproduced with applicant IDs to
ensure that the baseline and enhanced models use the same applicants.

```{r}
# Reproduce the original sample while retaining applicant IDs
set.seed(6812)

model_data_with_ids <- train_prepared |>
  dplyr::select(
    SK_ID_CURR,
    TARGET,
    dplyr::all_of(final_predictors)
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(TARGET = as.integer(TARGET)) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    dplyr::if_all(
      -c(SK_ID_CURR, TARGET),
      ~ !is.na(.) & is.finite(.)
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(TARGET) |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(
    prop = 10000 / nrow(train_prepared)
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

# Verify that the original sample was reproduced
stopifnot(
  identical(
    dplyr::select(model_data_with_ids, -SK_ID_CURR),
    model_data
  )
)

# Add Bureau features to the matched applicants
bureau_sample <- model_data_with_ids |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    bureau_features,
    by = "SK_ID_CURR"
  )

# Verify that no applicants were duplicated
stopifnot(nrow(bureau_sample) == nrow(model_data))

# Check the result
dim(bureau_sample)
```

### Handle Missing Bureau Information

Applicants without Bureau records are retained. A missing-history
indicator identifies these applicants, while missing numeric Bureau
features will be imputed within each training fold.

```{r}
bureau_sample <- bureau_sample |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(
      is.na(BUREAU_LOAN_COUNT)
    )
  )

# Check missing-history counts
table(bureau_sample$BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING)

# Check sample size
dim(bureau_sample)
```

### Three-Fold Cross-Validation Setup

Both models will use the same applicants and validation folds
to ensure a fair comparison.

```{r}
# Create three stratified folds
set.seed(6812)

bureau_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(
  bureau_sample,
  v = 3,
  strata = TARGET
)

# Verify the folds
bureau_folds
```

### Compare Baseline and Bureau-Enhanced Logistic Regression

Both models are evaluated using the same three stratified folds.
Missing Bureau values are handled using training-fold information
only to avoid data leakage.

```{r}
# Predictor lists
baseline_vars <- final_predictors

enhanced_vars <- c(
  baseline_vars,
  "BUREAU_LOAN_COUNT",
  "BUREAU_ACTIVE_COUNT",
  "BUREAU_TOTAL_DEBT",
  "BUREAU_MAX_OVERDUE_DAYS",
  "BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING"
)

# Calculate ROC AUC for one model and one fold
evaluate_logistic <- function(split, predictors) {

  training <- rsample::analysis(split)
  validation <- rsample::assessment(split)

  # Keep only the outcome and selected predictors
  training <- training |>
    dplyr::select(TARGET, dplyr::all_of(predictors))

  validation <- validation |>
    dplyr::select(TARGET, dplyr::all_of(predictors))

  # Impute missing values using training-fold medians
  for (variable in predictors) {

    missing_training <- is.na(training[[variable]]) |
      !is.finite(training[[variable]])

    missing_validation <- is.na(validation[[variable]]) |
      !is.finite(validation[[variable]])

    median_value <- median(
      training[[variable]][!missing_training],
      na.rm = TRUE
    )

    if (!is.finite(median_value)) {
      median_value <- 0
    }

    training[[variable]][missing_training] <- median_value
    validation[[variable]][missing_validation] <- median_value
  }

  # Train Logistic Regression
  model <- glm(
    TARGET ~ .,
    data = training,
    family = binomial()
  )

  # Predict payment-difficulty probabilities
  probabilities <- predict(
    model,
    newdata = validation,
    type = "response"
  )

  # Calculate ROC AUC
  as.numeric(
  pROC::auc(
    pROC::roc(
      response = validation$TARGET,
      predictor = probabilities,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      direction = "<",
      quiet = TRUE
    )
  )
)
}

# Evaluate both models on identical folds
bureau_cv_results <- purrr::map_dfr(
  seq_len(nrow(bureau_folds)),
  function(i) {

    split <- bureau_folds$splits[[i]]

    tibble::tibble(
      Fold = i,
      Baseline_AUC = evaluate_logistic(
        split, baseline_vars
      ),
      Bureau_AUC = evaluate_logistic(
        split, enhanced_vars
      )
    )
  }
)

# Compare results
bureau_cv_results <- bureau_cv_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Improvement = Bureau_AUC - Baseline_AUC
  )

bureau_cv_results

# Calculate average performance
bureau_cv_summary <- bureau_cv_results |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Baseline_Mean_AUC = mean(Baseline_AUC),
    Bureau_Mean_AUC = mean(Bureau_AUC),
    Mean_Improvement = mean(Improvement)
  )

bureau_cv_summary
```

### Previous Application Features

This experiment adds previous loan application information to
the Bureau-enhanced model to evaluate whether it improves ROC AUC.

```{r}
# Load and aggregate previous applications
previous <- readr::read_csv(
  "Data/previous_application.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

previous_features <- aggregate_previous_data(previous)

# Add previous application features
combined_sample <- bureau_sample |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    previous_features,
    by = "SK_ID_CURR"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    PREV_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(
      is.na(PREV_APP_COUNT)
    )
  )

# Verify that all original applicants remain
stopifnot(nrow(combined_sample) == nrow(bureau_sample))

# Check the resulting dataset
dim(combined_sample)
```

### Compare Bureau and Previous Application Features

Both models use the same three cross-validation folds.
Missing values are imputed using training-fold medians.

```{r}
# Bureau predictors from our previous experiment
bureau_vars <- enhanced_vars

# Add previous-application predictors
combined_vars <- c(
  bureau_vars,
  "PREV_APP_COUNT",
  "PREV_APPROVED_COUNT",
  "PREV_REFUSED_COUNT",
  "PREV_AVG_CREDIT",
  "PREV_HISTORY_MISSING"
)

# Evaluate both models using the same fold assignments
previous_cv_results <- purrr::map_dfr(
  seq_len(nrow(bureau_folds)),
  function(i) {

    split <- bureau_folds$splits[[i]]

    # Get original training and validation applicant IDs
    training_ids <- rsample::analysis(split)$SK_ID_CURR
    validation_ids <- rsample::assessment(split)$SK_ID_CURR

    # Find matching rows in the combined dataset
    training_rows <- match(
      training_ids,
      combined_sample$SK_ID_CURR
    )

    validation_rows <- match(
      validation_ids,
      combined_sample$SK_ID_CURR
    )

    # Ensure all applicants were matched
    stopifnot(
      !anyNA(training_rows),
      !anyNA(validation_rows)
    )

    # Recreate the same fold with additional features
    combined_split <- rsample::make_splits(
      list(
        analysis = training_rows,
        assessment = validation_rows
      ),
      combined_sample
    )

    # Compare Bureau-only and combined models
    tibble::tibble(
      Fold = i,

      Bureau_AUC = evaluate_logistic(
        combined_split,
        bureau_vars
      ),

      Combined_AUC = evaluate_logistic(
        combined_split,
        combined_vars
      )
    )
  }
)

# Calculate improvement for each fold
previous_cv_results <- previous_cv_results |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    Improvement = Combined_AUC - Bureau_AUC
  )

# Display fold results

  )
```

### Compare Models With and Without Installment Features

This experiment compares the existing model (Application, Bureau, and Previous Application features) with an enhanced model that also includes Installment Payment features.

Both models use the same applicants and three stratified cross-validation folds. Missing values are imputed using medians calculated from each training fold to prevent data leakage.

```{r}
# Existing predictors from previous experiments
existing_predictors <- c(
  final_predictors,
  "BUREAU_LOAN_COUNT",
  "BUREAU_ACTIVE_COUNT",
  "BUREAU_TOTAL_DEBT",
  "BUREAU_MAX_OVERDUE_DAYS",
  "BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING",
  "PREV_APP_COUNT",
  "PREV_APPROVED_COUNT",
  "PREV_REFUSED_COUNT",
  "PREV_AVG_CREDIT",
  "PREV_HISTORY_MISSING"
)

# Add installment payment predictors
installment_predictors <- c(
  existing_predictors,
  "INST_PAYMENT_COUNT",
  "INST_LATE_PAYMENT_RATE",
  "INST_AVG_PAYMENT_DELAY",
  "INST_TOTAL_SHORTFALL",
  "INST_HISTORY_MISSING"
)

# Create three stratified folds using the enhanced dataset
set.seed(6812)

installment_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(
  installment_sample,
  v = 3,
  strata = TARGET
)

# Compare both models using identical validation folds
installment_cv_results <- purrr::map_dfr(
  seq_len(nrow(installment_folds)),
  function(i) {

    split <- installment_folds$splits[[i]]

    # Existing model without installment features
    existing_auc <- evaluate_logistic(
      split,
      existing_predictors
    )

    # Enhanced model with installment features
    installment_auc <- evaluate_logistic(
      split,
      installment_predictors
    )

    tibble::tibble(
      Fold = i,
      Existing_AUC = existing_auc,
      Installment_AUC = installment_auc,
      Improvement = installment_auc - existing_auc
    )
  }
)

# Display ROC AUC for each fold
installment_cv_results

# Calculate average ROC AUC
installment_cv_summary <- installment_cv_results |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Existing_Mean_AUC = mean(Existing_AUC),

  )
```

## Final Enhanced Model

The final enhanced Logistic Regression model combines application information with Bureau credit history, previous applications, installment payments, POS/CASH balances, and credit card history. After re-evaluating predictor selection, three additional variables EXT_SOURCE_1, EXT_SOURCE_2, and EXT_SOURCE_3 were incorporated to improve predictive performance, bringing the total number of predictors to 36.

### Prepare Full Training Data

```{r}
# Combine all supplementary datasets with the full training data
enhanced_train <- train_prepared |>
  dplyr::left_join(bureau_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(previous_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(installment_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(pos_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(credit_card_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(BUREAU_LOAN_COUNT)),
    PREV_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(PREV_APP_COUNT)),
    INST_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(INST_PAYMENT_COUNT)),
    POS_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(POS_RECORD_COUNT)),
    CC_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(CC_RECORD_COUNT))
  )

# Verify that all training applicants are retained
stopifnot(nrow(enhanced_train) == nrow(train_prepared))

# Inspect the enhanced dataset
dim(enhanced_train)

# Check missing-history indicators
enhanced_train |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Bureau_Missing = sum(BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING),
    Previous_Missing = sum(PREV_HISTORY_MISSING),
    Installment_Missing = sum(INST_HISTORY_MISSING),
    POS_Missing = sum(POS_HISTORY_MISSING),
    Credit_Card_Missing = sum(CC_HISTORY_MISSING)
  )
```

### Train Enhanced Logistic Regression

```{r}
# Use all predictors from our credit card experiment
enhanced_predictors <- unique(c(
  credit_card_predictors,
  "EXT_SOURCE_1",
  "EXT_SOURCE_2",
  "EXT_SOURCE_3"
))

# Select target and predictors
enhanced_model_data <- enhanced_train |>
  dplyr::select(TARGET, dplyr::all_of(enhanced_predictors)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(TARGET = as.integer(TARGET))

# Replace missing or infinite values using training medians
enhanced_medians <- sapply(
  enhanced_model_data[enhanced_predictors],
  function(x) {
    x[!is.finite(x)] <- NA_real_
    median_value <- median(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (!is.finite(median_value)) median_value <- 0
    median_value
  }
)

for (variable in enhanced_predictors) {
  missing_values <- !is.finite(enhanced_model_data[[variable]])

  enhanced_model_data[[variable]][missing_values] <-
    enhanced_medians[[variable]]
}

# Train on the full dataset
enhanced_model <- glm(
  TARGET ~ .,
  data = enhanced_model_data,
  family = binomial()
)

# Verify training size
nrow(enhanced_model_data)

# Check model fit
enhanced_model$converged
coef(enhanced_model)
```

### External Credit Score Experiment

The previous enhanced Logistic Regression model used 33 predictors
from the application and supplementary credit-history datasets.

To improve predictive performance, three additional variables
were introduced: EXT_SOURCE_1, EXT_SOURCE_2, and EXT_SOURCE_3.

Both models were evaluated using five-fold stratified
cross-validation on the full training dataset of 307,511 applicants.
Missing predictor values were imputed using medians calculated
from each training fold.

```{r}
# Create five stratified folds
set.seed(123)

enhanced_folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(
  enhanced_train,
  v = 5,
  strata = TARGET
)

# Evaluate original 33-predictor model
auc_33 <- sapply(
  enhanced_folds$splits,
  evaluate_logistic,
  predictors = credit_card_predictors
)

# Evaluate updated 36-predictor model
auc_36 <- sapply(
  enhanced_folds$splits,
  evaluate_logistic,
  predictors = enhanced_predictors
)
```

```{r}
# Compare the original and updated models
validation_comparison <- tibble::tibble(
  Fold = 1:5,
  Original_33_AUC = auc_33,
  Updated_36_AUC = auc_36,
  Improvement = auc_36 - auc_33
)

validation_comparison

# Summarize results
validation_summary <- tibble::tibble(
  Model = c("Original 33 Predictors", "Updated 36 Predictors"),
  Mean_AUC = c(mean(auc_33), mean(auc_36)),
  SD_AUC = c(sd(auc_33), sd(auc_36))
)

validation_summary
```

The original 33-predictor model achieved a mean ROC AUC of 0.6866,
while the updated 36-predictor model achieved 0.7481.

The average improvement was 0.0616 AUC points. Performance
improved in all five validation folds, indicating that the
external credit scores contribute meaningful predictive information.

### Prepare Enhanced Kaggle Test Data

```{r}
# Join supplementary features to the Kaggle test data
enhanced_test <- test_prepared |>
  dplyr::left_join(bureau_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(previous_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(installment_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(pos_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::left_join(credit_card_features, by = "SK_ID_CURR") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    BUREAU_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(BUREAU_LOAN_COUNT)),
    PREV_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(PREV_APP_COUNT)),
    INST_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(INST_PAYMENT_COUNT)),
    POS_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(POS_RECORD_COUNT)),
    CC_HISTORY_MISSING = as.integer(is.na(CC_RECORD_COUNT))
  )

# Confirm all test applicants are retained
stopifnot(nrow(enhanced_test) == nrow(test_prepared))

# Select the same predictors used during training
enhanced_test_model <- enhanced_test |>
  dplyr::select(dplyr::all_of(enhanced_predictors))

# Impute missing values using TRAINING medians
for (variable in enhanced_predictors) {
  missing_values <- !is.finite(enhanced_test_model[[variable]])

  enhanced_test_model[[variable]][missing_values] <-
    enhanced_medians[[variable]]
}

# Verify dimensions and missing values
dim(enhanced_test_model)
sum(is.na(enhanced_test_model))

# Examine applicant 100067
applicant_row <- which(enhanced_test$SK_ID_CURR == 100067)

applicant_values <- enhanced_test_model[applicant_row, , drop = FALSE]

# Calculate each predictor's contribution to the prediction
applicant_contributions <- as.numeric(applicant_values[1, ]) *
  coef(enhanced_model)[-1]

contribution_table <- data.frame(
  Predictor = names(coef(enhanced_model))[-1],
  Contribution = applicant_contributions
)

contribution_table <- contribution_table[
  order(abs(contribution_table$Contribution), decreasing = TRUE),
]

head(contribution_table, 10)

# Verify applicant 100067's predicted probability
predict(enhanced_model, newdata = applicant_values, type = "response")
```

## Kaggle Evaluation Results

Three Logistic Regression models were submitted to the Home Credit Default Risk competition on Kaggle. The initial model used six predictors, the enhanced model incorporated 33 predictors, and the revised model included 36 predictors after adding EXT_SOURCE_1, EXT_SOURCE_2, and EXT_SOURCE_3.

| Model | Public ROC AUC | Private ROC AUC |
|---|---:|---:|
| Initial Logistic Regression (6 predictors) | 0.62268 | 0.60727 |
| Enhanced Logistic Regression (33 predictors) | 0.69607 | 0.68375 |
| Updated Logistic Regression (36 predictors) | 0.74751 | 0.73212 |

The public and private AUC values above are documented from the original Kaggle evaluation. The local submission CSV files available in this project do not independently verify the recorded 36-predictor scores.

The initial Logistic Regression model achieved a public Kaggle ROC AUC of 0.62268 and a private ROC AUC of 0.60727.

Adding features from five supplementary credit-history datasets improved performance to 0.69607 (public) and 0.68375 (private).

After re-evaluating predictor selection, three additional variables—EXT_SOURCE_1, EXT_SOURCE_2, and EXT_SOURCE_3—were incorporated into the enhanced model.

The revised 36-predictor Logistic Regression model achieved a public Kaggle ROC AUC of **0.74751** and a private ROC AUC of **0.73212**. Five-fold cross-validation on the full training dataset produced a mean ROC AUC of approximately **0.748**.

These results demonstrate that incorporating the external credit score predictors substantially improved the model's ability to distinguish applicants who experience payment difficulties from those who do not.

## Model Limitations

Although the revised 36-predictor Logistic Regression model achieved a mean five-fold cross-validation ROC AUC of 0.748, its Kaggle public and private ROC AUC scores were 0.74751 and 0.73212, respectively. This difference indicates that predictive performance can vary across evaluation datasets.

The dataset is highly imbalanced, with approximately 8.1% of applicants experiencing payment difficulties. Although ROC AUC is useful for evaluating discrimination under class imbalance, additional metrics such as precision, recall, and the precision-recall curve would provide a more complete assessment.

The initial supplementary feature experiments used approximately 10,000 applicants and three-fold cross-validation to reduce computational requirements. The final comparison between the 33-predictor and 36-predictor models used the full training dataset of 307,511 applicants with five-fold stratified cross-validation, providing a more comprehensive evaluation.

Another limitation is the use of Logistic Regression, which may not fully capture nonlinear relationships between financial variables. More advanced approaches, such as gradient boosting, could potentially improve predictive performance.

Finally, because this model concerns lending decisions, predictive performance alone would not be sufficient for real-world deployment. Fairness, interpretability, probability calibration, and the consequences of incorrect predictions would also need to be evaluated.

## Conclusion

This project explored how predictive modeling can help Home Credit identify applicants who are more likely to experience payment difficulties. Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest models were compared using cross-validation and ROC AUC. Logistic Regression performed best among the initial models tested.

The initial six-predictor Logistic Regression model achieved a public Kaggle ROC AUC of 0.62268 and a private ROC AUC of 0.60727. Adding information from five supplementary datasets—Bureau, Previous Applications, Installment Payments, POS/CASH Balance, and Credit Card Balance—improved performance to 0.69607 (public) and 0.68375 (private).

After re-evaluating predictor selection, three additional variables—EXT_SOURCE_1, EXT_SOURCE_2, and EXT_SOURCE_3—were incorporated into the enhanced model. The revised 36-predictor Logistic Regression model achieved a mean five-fold cross-validation ROC AUC of **0.748**, a public Kaggle ROC AUC of **0.74751**, and a private Kaggle ROC AUC of **0.73212**.

These results demonstrate that selecting informative predictors can substantially improve predictive performance. In particular, the external credit score variables provided valuable information beyond the original application and historical credit features.

From a business perspective, improved risk predictions could help lenders identify higher-risk applicants and support more informed lending decisions. However, additional evaluation of fairness, interpretability, and model reliability would be necessary before real-world implementation.

Future improvements could include testing gradient boosting models, engineering additional predictors, and evaluating precision, recall, and probability calibration.
